newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE--Brazil to discuss future at industry forum.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Brazil to discuss future at industry forum.

text.p: Leaders of the various entities within Brazil's coffee community will next week descend on a beach resort hotel in the state of Bahia to discuss the way forward for Brazil's coffee policy.

The talks, organised by Brazil's Coffee Industry Association (ABIC) which represents roasters, will run alongside ABIC's annual forum on prospects for the future and will involve around 40 key figures, said ABIC secretary-general David Nahum.
"We will broach all the key issues such as crop surveys, stocks, marketing, producer debts, participation in international bodies," Nahum said.
"But these are informal talks, there will not be a final document," he added.

The forum is to take place from November 27 to December 1 on Ilha de Comandatuba near Ilheus in Bahia state and in total should involve around 540 industry representatives and their families, Nahum said.

Apart from representatives from the exporting, producing and industry sectors, officials from the Industry and Commerce Ministry including Mauricio Assis, head of the primary commodities department and Jose Monteiro, head of the National Coffee Department will take part in talks on the way ahead.
Also attending will be Celsius Lodder, executive director of the International Coffee Organisation, Rubens Barbosa, head of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) and ACPC
secretary-general Roberio Oliveira.

The meeting comes shortly after the creation of a new coffee council, the CDPC, which unites the private and public sectors and which will be responsible for shaping policy in the future. "I think the timing of the meeting is very good and people will be going to discuss medium and long-term ideas," said Oswaldo Aranha, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters" Federation.
Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles who is also head of the council cannot attend the event so there can be no formal session of the new council.
But ABIC president Jose Carlos da Silva was optimistic a date for the first meeting would be agreed next week.
On the roasters' side, the industry is concerned about supply in the coming years, given the continued growth in domestic demand which this year is seen at 11 million bags.
This is expected to grow to 12 million bags in 1997, with ABIC still working to a goal of 15 million by the year 2000.
"We are worried about the future...Brazil has a huge
potential and we have to increase production not only to meet growing internal consumption but also to recuperate Brazil's place in the international market," da Silva said.

In the long-term, da Silva said that roasters would like to see production of 35 million bags by the start of next century but of immediate concern is supply in the first half of next year when Brazil in theory should export six million bags of coffee under an agreement with other ACPC members.
Already traders and roasters are calling for the government to increase the size of its monthly auctions in order to guarantee export levels and internal supply.

Although the maximum limit for each sale is currently 200,000 bags, the largest auction so far has been 85,466 bags. "From January however auctions should become larger. We will negotiate with the government within the CDPC," da Silva said.
The 200,000 bag limit should be sufficient to meet needs in the first quarter of next year but may need to be re-evaluated in the April to June period, he added.
-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
